sections.body: Several sources treat real-time rendering as a problem of spending limited computation where it matters most. ReSTIR improves many-light direct illumination by raising direct-light sample quality before denoising, while foveated rendering allocates high quality to the foveal region and lower quality to the periphery.
sections.heading: Quality budgets

sections.body: The evidence supports a synthesis around quality budgets: statistical estimators, perceptual models, and rendering paradigms all choose where approximation is acceptable and where missing detail, latency, or discontinuities become visible.
sections.heading: Shared synthesis

sections.body: The comparison should remain bounded: ReSTIR's evidence concerns light-sample selection and estimator behavior, while foveated rendering's evidence concerns human-visual-system models and regional quality variation.
sections.heading: Boundaries

title: Sample Quality and Perceptual Quality Allocation
